narrative: The model estimated a 51.0% chance that you will fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is just over half, your application was treated as a likely first-attempt bar failure and was denied; it is a close call, not a certainty. The strongest factor was your undergraduate grade point average. At 3.30 it was slightly above the 3.23 average among accepted students, and it pushed the prediction toward passing. The second most influential factor was your third-year class standing. You were in the second decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, and this worked against you by increasing the estimated risk of bar failure. The third factor was your family income bracket. Being from a lower-middle-income family slightly favored a passing outcome. Even though your GPA and income bracket helped, your low third-year standing was weighted heavily enough that the overall estimate landed just over the failure line. To improve a future application, focus on strengthening your academic record, especially later-year grades, and seek advising on bar-exam preparation. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it from 28 toward the accepted average of about 37, and ask admissions staff which parts of your file you can most realistically improve before reapplying.
